greeting: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Grace and peace be with you all as we gather in the presence of our merciful God.
penitential:
Lord Jesus, you lead your people beside restful waters: Lord, have mercy.
You are our shepherd and guide in the dark valley: Christ, have mercy.
You prepare a banquet for us in your eternal kingdom: Lord, have_mercy.
psalm_response: The Lord is my shepherd; there is nothing I shall want.
homily:
We begin today with something very simple and very concrete: a dusty road in Samaria and Galilee, and ten men standing at a distance. Think of them for a moment. They are not close to the crowd; they are separated by the rules of their world, standing far off, their voices raised together in a desperate, unified cry: 'Jesus, Master! Have pity on us!' They do not have much left to offer the world, only their need, only their shared ache. They are living in the margins, watching the world move by without them, waiting for a word that might change everything. When Jesus looks at them, He does not turn away or lecture them on how they arrived at that dusty crossroads. He simply gives a command: 'Go show yourselves to the priests.' And as they walk—step by step, putting one foot in front of the other down that uncertain road—the healing meets them. They are cleansed while they are moving.

I want you to hold onto this image: walking down the road while the healing happens. It is the image of a journey where we do not have to have all the answers before we take the next step. It is the quiet movement of faith, where grace meets us not when we are standing still in our despair, but precisely when we are moving forward, trusting the word we have been given.

Let us tell the truth of the heart before we look for the comfort. Alan, Thao, Ryan, and all of you who hold the memory of Benjamin as a sacred trust: it has been four months since he went home to God. We know the reality of your quiet house. We know the moments when the silence becomes a weight, when the habits of a lifetime—the brilliant, curious mind that loved to explore the architecture of the world, the gentle, respectful spirit that made him such a treasure—are suddenly interrupted by the sharp, cold realization that he is not there in the way he once was. You are grieving. You are carrying a cross that is heavy, real, and unrelenting. You are allowed to be tired. You are allowed to feel the sudden ache when a memory ambushes you in the middle of an ordinary Tuesday. Do not pretend the weight is lighter than it is.

And let us gently lift one particular stone from your hearts today—a stone that grief often slips into our pockets without us noticing. Sometimes, when a family suffers an unimaginable loss, the mind begins to circle back, whispering quiet, unfair questions. Did we miss a sign? Could we have done something more? Could we have watched closer? Let us lay that burden down right here at the altar. You missed nothing. You loved Benjamin with a completeness that filled his fifteen years with the richness of a lifetime—traveling the globe together, sharing quiet stories, and walking side by side. You were the exact parents and the exact brother that Benjamin needed. Let that heavy stone fall; you are absolved, and you are held. You did not fail him in any way. You were the light in his life, just as he was the light in yours. Some things in this life are simply beyond our control, and God does not hold you responsible for the mysteries of the cross. You are held in His mercy, not judged by your sorrow.

Now, let the Gospel break into that quiet room. Listen to what happens after the ten are cleansed: 'And one of them, realizing he had been healed, returned, glorifying God in a loud voice; and he fell at the feet of Jesus and thanked him.' Out of ten, only one turns back. Only one realizes that the gift cannot simply be consumed; it must be acknowledged, received, and brought back to the Giver. Benjamin was a boy who understood this kind of gratitude, this wide-eyed appreciation for the gifts of life. Think of how he moved through the world with such eager curiosity. Think of his passion for aviation, how he loved to look at airplanes, dreaming of his ‘con chim airlines’ and giggling with pure joy when he talked about it. He wasn't just looking at metal and engines; he was looking at the wonder of the skies, looking for the beauty that God had poured into creation. He had that rare gift of noticing the world and finding delight in it. 

Consider the first reading from St. Paul to Titus: 'When the kindness and generous love of God our savior appeared, not because of any righteous deeds we had done but because of his mercy, he saved us through the bath of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit.' Paul reminds us that our standing before God is not earned by our perfection, but received as a pure gift of His mercy. Benjamin’s life was a reflection of that generous love. Think of the extraordinary depth of his heart—that moment when, unprompted, he told his parents he was willing to give up his entire piggy bank to help his uncle William, who was suffering. He didn't need to break it open; the offer itself revealed the magnificent generosity of his soul. He was a boy whose heart was already sized for eternity. He was a boy who knew that the true wealth of life is not what we keep, but what we are willing to offer for the sake of those we love. That love is still flowing, echoing in quiet acts of kindness across the world, proving that a life given in love never truly ends.

Ryan, you are a brother who carries a unique, holy weight. You know the memories better than anyone. You know the shared laughter, the everyday life of being brothers, the quiet moments that no one else saw. You are not just a brother who remains; you are a brother who continues the story. When you look at the sky, when you think of the future, remember that you are not doing it alone. You are carrying the legacy of his joy. You are a witness to the world that love is not a finite resource. It is a well that never runs dry. Keep being the boy who reaches out. Keep being the one who values the small, human moments. You are a vital part of this family of four, and your life is a testament to the fact that love is the most durable thing we possess. Your brother's love is not gone; it is woven into the very fabric of who you are becoming.

We hear in the Psalm today: 'The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. In verdant pastures he gives me repose; Beside restful waters he leads me; he refreshes my soul.' This is the turn of the heart. The Good Shepherd does not abandon His flock in the dark valley. He walks right into it. He carries the staff and the rod that give us courage. Benjamin is now resting in those verdant pastures. He is dwelling in the house of the Lord for years to come, exactly as the Psalm promises. He is not lost to you; he is held safely in the arms of the ultimate Shepherd.

Think of the dream you had, Alan, where you and Ben were waiting in line to buy ice cream, and Ben paid. That is the image of the kingdom. It is the image of the one who has gone before us, stepping forward with generosity and love, watching over you. He is well, he is strong, and he is waiting with that same gentle smile you remember so well. He is the one who has already crossed the threshold into the light, and he is cheering you on.

To everyone listening from afar—especially other children who are carrying heavy crosses of suffering, and every family whose home feels too quiet today—hear this: you are seen by God. You are not forgotten. The Lord draws closest to the brokenhearted.

So, what do you carry out the door today? Not a summary, not a heavy burden, but one small, doable thing: when the grief rises and the house feels too quiet, pause. Close your eyes. Breathe in. Imagine the Lord leading you beside restful waters, and imagine Benjamin standing nearby, smiling that bright, joyful grin, looking out toward an endless horizon. Let yourself be gathered into the peace of Christ. Walk out knowing that you are loved, that you are not to blame, and that the one who went before you is waiting at the door of eternity. You are a family of four, held in the palm of God's hand, now and forever. Amen.
spiritual_communion: My Jesus, I believe that You are present in the Most Holy Sacrament. I love You above all things, and I desire to receive You into my soul. Since I cannot at this moment receive You sacramentally, come at least spiritually into my heart. I embrace You as if You were already there and unite myself wholly to You. Never permit me to be separated from You. Amen.
closing: May the Lord bless you and keep you, and may His gentle peace sustain you this day and always. Amen.
standing_petitions: For a boy named Ben and all who have died, that they rest in the light of Christ, we pray to the Lord.
For all who grieve, that God console them and give them hope, we pray to the Lord.

readings.label: Reading 1
readings.text:
Beloved:
Remind them to be under the control of magistrates and authorities,
to be obedient, to be open to every good enterprise.
They are to slander no one, to be peaceable, considerate,
exercising all graciousness toward everyone.
For we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, deluded,
slaves to various desires and pleasures,
living in malice and envy,
hateful ourselves and hating one another.But when the kindness and generous love
of God our savior appeared,
not because of any righteous deeds we had done
but because of his mercy,
he saved us through the bath of rebirth
and renewal by the Holy Spirit,
whom he richly poured out on us
through Jesus Christ our savior,
so that we might be justified by his grace
and become heirs in hope of eternal life.

readings.label: Responsorial Psalm
readings.text:
R.    (1) The Lord is my shepherd; there is nothing I shall want.
The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.
In verdant pastures he gives me repose;
Beside restful waters he leads me;
he refreshes my soul.
R.    The Lord is my shepherd; there is nothing I shall want.
He guides me in right paths
for his name’s sake.
Even though I walk in the dark valley
I fear no evil; for you are at my side
With your rod and your staff
that give me courage.
R.    The Lord is my shepherd; there is nothing I shall want.
You spread the table before me
in the sight of my foes;
You anoint my head with oil;
my cup overflows.
R.    The Lord is my shepherd; there is nothing I shall want.
Only goodness and kindness follow me
all the days of my life;
And I shall dwell in the house of the LORD
for years to come.
R.    The Lord is my shepherd; there is nothing I shall want.

readings.label: Gospel
readings.text:
As Jesus continued his journey to Jerusalem,
he traveled through Samaria and Galilee.
As he was entering a village, ten lepers met him.
They stood at a distance from him and raised their voice, saying,
“Jesus, Master! Have pity on us!”
And when he saw them, he said,
“Go show yourselves to the priests.”
As they were going they were cleansed.
And one of them, realizing he had been healed,
returned, glorifying God in a loud voice;
and he fell at the feet of Jesus and thanked him.
He was a Samaritan.
Jesus said in reply,
“Ten were cleansed, were they not?
Where are the other nine?
Has none but this foreigner returned to give thanks to God?”
Then he said to him, “Stand up and go;
your faith has saved you.”

pet_prayers.text: Ben, my sweet boy, I miss you so much. Thank you for visiting me and Chú Chris last night. He told me he saw you flying a helicopter—so free, joyful, and strong up there. Down here, Mom and I are crying more and more each day. A piece of my heart feels completely dead without you, Ben. Please watch over us, pray for your mom, your brother Ryan, and me, and give us the strength to keep going. We love you forever
